The worst one was the November 2024 consumer-lag incident on Skeinrouter, our Kafka-based shipment tracking pipeline. We were four weeks into a per-carrier rollout with 720 carriers live when a routine rolling restart of the 16 projector pods started. Lag on the tracking topic began climbing almost immediately, and I took incident command when we declared Sev-2 about fifteen minutes in. It escalated to Sev-1 about an hour later, with lag peaking at 96 million events and the worst-hit shipments running 47 minutes behind.

The root cause was a rebalance storm. The consumer group still used eager rebalancing, so every pod restart stopped the entire group. While the database absorbed the backlog, batches started exceeding the 30-second max poll interval, members got evicted for being slow, and each eviction triggered another rebalance. We paused the deploy, scaled the group down to 8 pods, and raised the max poll interval to 5 minutes, which stabilized things. The backlog drained by 17:45, and we closed the incident after 3 hours 40 minutes. No events were lost and nothing rolled back, the deduplication table kept duplicates out.

The follow-up was the part I care about most. We moved every consumer group to cooperative rebalancing with static membership, made rolling restarts go one pod at a time behind a lag gate, and added burn-rate alerts on consumer lag. That work was finished by early December, and it's why the system has stayed boring since.

I'm primary on-call one week in five for the dispatch domain at Quillhaven, and I've been incident commander for nine Sev-1 and Sev-2 incidents since April 2024. The load has come down a lot: we cut Sev-1s from 14 in 2023 to 5 in 2025, and median time to restore from 52 minutes to 19.

## Approach
Two-pointer scan from both ends. I skip any character that isn't an ASCII letter or digit, then compare the remaining pair case-insensitively. If the pointers ever meet or cross, it's a palindrome.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1

    while left < right:
        while left < right and not s[left].isalnum():
            left += 1
        while left < right and not s[right].isalnum():
            right -= 1

        if s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():
            return False

        left += 1
        right -= 1

    return True
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n) since each character is visited at most once. Space is O(1), just the two pointers.

SMS is 5% of 180 million notifications per day, so **9 million SMS messages daily**. Averaged over 86,400 seconds that is about **104 messages per second**. Peak load is 6 times the average, so **625 messages per second at peak**.

The SMS vendor accepts at most **500 messages per second**. So at peak, demand is 625 against a 500 capacity, a shortfall of **125 messages per second**. The vendor cannot keep up at peak, and I need a buffer.

The buffer is a queue in front of the vendor. The vendor drains it at 500 per second, and the excess 125 per second accumulates during the burst. If a campaign burst lasts an hour, that is 125 times 3,600, or **450,000 messages** queued. The outbox pattern solves the problem of keeping two systems in sync when you can't do both operations in one transaction. from collections import Counter
```python
import heapq

def top_k_words(words, k):
    counts = Counter(words)
    heap = []
    for word, count in counts.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (count, word))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    result = []
    while heap:
        count, word = heapq.heappop(heap)
        result.append(word)
    return result[::-1]
```

They're not the same algorithm. The problem sheet limiter is a sliding window: it keeps the timestamps of the last `limit` allowed requests and drops old ones as the window moves, so a request is judged against the exact requests in the trailing `window` milliseconds. The Go tracker is a fixed window: it just counts units per tenant and resets the whole counter when the window ends.

The practical difference is burst behavior. With a fixed window, a tenant can use the entire limit at the very end of one window and again at the very start of the next, so two full bursts can land back to back. The sliding window spreads that out, because old requests age out continuously instead of all at once. The Go tracker also has a race: it reads the count, checks the limit, then writes under a separate lock, so two concurrent requests can both pass the check and overshoot the limit. The sheet's limiter is single-threaded over a sorted list, so it doesn't have that problem. [[GIST]] Fixed window resets in bursts; sliding window ages requests out

I'd reach for a read-write lock when reads dominate and the critical section is long enough that letting readers run concurrently actually pays off. A plain mutex serializes everything, so if I have many goroutines mostly reading shared state and only occasional writers, an RWMutex lets all those readers proceed at once and only excludes them during a write.

It isn't worth it when the critical section is tiny, like a map lookup or a counter increment. The overhead of the RWMutex itself, plus the cache-line contention on the lock word, can cost more than the work being protected. It's also a poor fit when reads and writes are roughly balanced, because writers still need exclusive access and readers can starve them. In those cases a plain mutex is simpler and often faster.

```python
def fixed_window_allowed(timestamps, limit, window):
    if not timestamps:

    result = []

        bucket = t // window
```
